title: File Storage Design
description: Design a scalable file storage system with object storage, CDN delivery, metadata indexing, and chunked uploads for large files.

data.text: File storage systems must support uploads, downloads, metadata management, and fast content delivery. Products like Google Drive, Dropbox, and S3 store exabytes of data while serving millions of requests per second. In interviews, file storage design tests your ability to integrate object storage, CDNs, and database indexing while handling large files and concurrent access.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Upload and download files of any size
Store metadata such as file name, size, type, and owner
Support sharing, permissions, and version control
Stream large files without loading the entire object into memory

data.text: Object storage systems like S3 store files as binary objects in buckets. Unlike file systems, object storage does not support directories or random writes. Every write creates a new version of the object, and updates replace the previous version. Use content-addressed storage with hashes as identifiers to detect duplicate uploads and enable deduplication across the system.

Files larger than a few hundred megabytes should be split into smaller chunks for resumable uploads. The client uploads each chunk independently to an upload session. Once all chunks are uploaded, the server assembles them into the final object. This approach allows users to pause and resume uploads, recover from network failures, and upload in parallel for higher throughput.

data.caption: Chunked upload flow for large files
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as API Server
    participant O as Object Storage
    participant M as Metadata DB
    C->>A: Initiate multipart upload
    A->>M: Create upload session
    M-->>A: Session ID + upload URLs
    A-->>C: Session ID + presigned chunk URLs
    loop For each chunk

data.text: A CDN caches file content at edge locations close to users. Configure cache TTLs based on file mutability. Images, videos, and static documents can have long cache lifetimes. Use cache-busting with file version hashes when content changes. Set appropriate Content-Type and Content-Disposition headers so browsers handle files correctly. Enable range request support so video players can seek to specific timestamps.

data.title: Security and access control
data.text: Never expose bucket URLs directly. Use presigned URLs that expire after a short time. Validate file types on the server and scan uploads for malware before storing them. Encrypt data at rest and in transit.

Store file metadata in a relational database like PostgreSQL. Metadata includes the file name, size, MIME type, owner ID, bucket path, upload timestamp, and sharing permissions. Index the owner ID and parent folder ID for fast directory listings. For high-scale systems, denormalize frequently accessed metadata into Redis and back it with the database as the source of truth.

Use optimistic concurrency with version numbers or ETags to handle simultaneous uploads. If two clients upload different versions of the same file, present both versions and allow the user to merge or choose. For shared documents, implement operational transforms or conflict-free replicated data types to merge concurrent edits without losing data.

terms.definition: A storage architecture that manages data as objects in buckets rather than files in a hierarchy.
A time-limited, signed URL that grants temporary access to upload or download an object without exposing credentials.
A technique that splits a large file into smaller parts uploaded independently, enabling resumable and parallel transfers.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use object storage for binary files and a relational database for metadata
Chunk large uploads to enable resumability and parallel transfers
Deliver files through a CDN with presigned URLs for security
Use cache-busting and version hashes to control cache invalidation
Handle concurrent uploads with optimistic concurrency and versioning
data.takeaway: A scalable file storage system combines durable object storage, fast metadata queries, and intelligent caching to deliver files instantly around the world.

items.question: How do you handle duplicate uploads?
items.answer: Compute a SHA-256 hash of the file at upload time. If the hash already exists in storage, skip the upload and return the existing file path. This deduplication can save significant storage costs.

items.question: What is the recommended chunk size for multipart uploads?
items.answer: Use 5 MB to 100 MB chunks. Smaller chunks reduce wasted bandwidth on retries, while larger chunks reduce the number of API calls. S3 recommends 5 MB to 100 MB per part.
